common_name: Wagnerianus Windmill Palm (Compact Stiff-Leaved Windmill Palm)
subcategory: cold-hardy fan palm for temperate gardens

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Wagnerianus is a smaller, stiffer-leaved variety of windmill palm with notably better wind tolerance than the species, since its shorter, tougher fronds resist tearing and shredding in storms.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade. Wagnerianus is a compact variety of windmill palm bearing smaller, stiffer, more rigid fan fronds than the species form, a trait that makes it noticeably more resistant to wind damage and shredding in storms, a real advantage along the Gulf Coast where tropical storm winds are a regular hazard for broad-leaved palms. It shares the species' excellent cold hardiness, tolerating temperatures into the single digits Fahrenheit once established, and its smaller, tidier crown fits narrower planting spaces than the standard windmill palm. Water regularly while establishing, then reduce to occasional deep watering during dry spells, and remove old, dead fronds as they brown to keep the trunk tidy.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Palms for the Landscape
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Palms for Louisiana Landscapes

common_name: Takil Windmill Palm (Rare Cold-Hardy Himalayan Windmill Palm)
subcategory: cold-hardy fan palm for temperate gardens

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Takil is a rare, distinct windmill palm species native to high elevations in the Kumaon Himalayas, sought by palm collectors for cold hardiness that can exceed even the more common Trachycarpus fortunei.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade. Takil is a rare windmill palm species native to high-elevation forests in the Kumaon region of the Himalayas, distinct from the far more commonly planted Trachycarpus fortunei, and prized among palm enthusiasts pushing the limits of cold-hardy palm cultivation for its exceptional tolerance of cold, sometimes cited as comparable to or better than standard windmill palm. It develops a similar fiber-covered trunk and fan-shaped fronds but can be slower growing and harder to source than the common windmill palm. Water regularly while establishing, then reduce to occasional deep watering during dry spells, and remove old, dead fronds as they brown to keep the trunk tidy.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Palms for the Landscape

common_name: Blue Mediterranean Fan Palm (Silvery-Blue Atlas Mountain Fan Palm)
subcategory: cold-hardy fan palm for temperate gardens

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Mediterranean Fan Palm is a striking silvery-blue-leaved variety from the Atlas Mountains of Morocco, generally more cold hardy than the green species form of Mediterranean fan palm.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun. Blue Mediterranean Fan Palm is a striking silvery-blue-leaved form of Mediterranean fan palm originating from the Atlas Mountains of Morocco, offering the same clumping, multi-trunked, drought-tolerant habit as the green species but with the added ornamental value of powder-blue fronds that stand out dramatically against darker landscape plantings. It is often noted as somewhat more cold hardy than the plain green form, and like the species it is highly drought-tolerant once established and tolerates poor, sandy, or coastal soils. Water regularly the first year to establish, then only during extended dry spells, and remove old fronds as they brown to keep the clumping crown tidy.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Palms for the Landscape

common_name: Silver Saw Palmetto (Silvery-Blue Coastal Saw Palmetto)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Silver Saw Palmetto is a prized silvery-blue-leaved coastal-dune form of the native saw palmetto, distinct from the more common green form.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; saw palmetto tolerates poor, dry, or salty coastal soils exceptionally well once established. Silver Saw Palmetto is a striking silvery-blue-leaved form of the native saw palmetto, most commonly found naturally along coastal dunes, offering the same slow-growing, spreading, low-trunked or trunkless habit of the species with the added ornamental impact of icy-blue fan fronds that contrast beautifully with green landscape plantings. Like the species it is extremely tough, drought- and salt-tolerant, and long-lived, making it an excellent low-maintenance native accent for xeriscape and coastal Gulf South gardens. It is very slow-growing, so patience is needed for a young plant to reach a substantial size, and it requires almost no supplemental care once established beyond removal of old fronds.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Palms for the Landscape
